claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at.% Cu and annealing at 800°C for 2 hours will form nanoscale Cu-rich precipitates in the HEA matrix.
The Cu-rich precipitates will have coherent interfaces with the HEA matrix.
The proposed 800°C treatment is a sub-critical anneal for the unspecified HEA.
Cu-rich precipitates will act as conductive pathways because Cu has superior thermal conductivity.
The conductive pathways created by the precipitates will enhance the alloy's overall heat transfer.
Coherent precipitate–matrix interfaces will mitigate stress concentrations.
Mitigating stress concentrations will preserve structural integrity and mechanical stability under reactor loading.
The modified alloy will have approximately 10–20% higher thermal conductivity than the conventional intermediate-layer HEA.
The modified alloy will retain mechanical strength similar to that of the baseline HEA.
The modified alloy will retain ductility similar to that of the baseline HEA.
The conductivity and mechanical-property benefits will persist during operation at temperatures up to approximately 1000 K.
The benefits will persist under steady-state heat flux and cyclic mechanical loading typical of plasma-facing intermediate layers.
Extreme thermal transients may compromise the benefits of the Cu-rich precipitates.
High radiation doses may destabilize the Cu-rich precipitates and compromise their benefits.
The standard HEA intermediate layer has moderate heat-transfer capability and adequate structural integrity.
